newsitem.title: USA: US unlikely to grow as fast in future, Yellen says.
newsitem.headline: US unlikely to grow as fast in future, Yellen says.

text.p: The economy is unlikely to grow as quickly in the next few years as it has done in the last four, White House chief economist Janet Yellen said on Monday.
The economy has grown by 2.6 percent per year since 1992. That is faster than the economy's long-term potential rate of about 2.3 percent, she said.

"The question is can we continue to grow that quickly over the next few years, and I regret the answer I give is, probably not," she told a luncheon meeting sponsored by the Center for National Policy.

Yellen, who chairs the White House's Council of Economic Advisers, said that the full employment rate -- or the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) - has probably fallen in the last several years.
"Although I am uncertain about the precise level of NAIRU myself, I'm certainly persuaded that it has fallen over the last several years," she said.
While it is not clear why that has occurred, Yellen said that restrained health insurance costs and increased globalization may have played a role.

Yellen voiced hopes that continued tight labor markets will ultimately help to lower the full employment rate further by encouraging companies to invest in worker training and other measures to boost the skills of their employees.
The White House economist said that worker productivity is likely higher than suggested by the official data. But she doubted that productivity growth -- no matter how measured -- has picked up.
"There is no evidence which I'm aware at this point to show that pace (of productivity growth) has accelerated," Yellen said.
